newsitem.title: USA: Cash in US 401k retirement plans seen up 63 pct by.
newsitem.headline: Cash in US 401k retirement plans seen up 63 pct by.

text.p: Americans will pour in a whopping 63 percent more money into corporate retirement plans to take the total to a record $1.3 trillion by 2000, according to forecasts by pension experts.
Last year, more than 22.3 million individuals participated in so-called 401ks, tax-favored retirement plans in which workers contribute a fixed portion of wages.
This is 2.5 million more people than in 1994, according to data from Access Research.

U.S. stock markets are expected to be the main beneficiary of this wave of new cash, with mutual funds, especially those focussing on stocks, gaining popularity as the investment of choice, experts predicted.
With all that growth, a battle is raging between retail and institutional money managers over who will get control of managing the pension money.

Total 401k assets, which have exploded in the last decade, will keep mushrooming. By the year 2000, U.S. 401k assets are forecast to grow to $1.3 trillion, up from $800 billion in 1996, $300 billion in 1990, and $155 billion in 1986, according to Cerulli Associates, a Boston consulting firm.
Cash flowing into mutual funds will also keep rising, according to Cerulli, to 44 percent of assets by 2000, up from 38 percent in 1996, 13 percent in 1990, and nine percent in 1986.

"401K assets are increasingly going into mutual funds, both through plans managed by fund companies, as well as plans managed by other providers, like insurers and banks," said Jeff Close, vice president of marketing at Access Research, a financial services consulting firm.
Within the 401k marketplace, retail firms are the market leaders, but they face stiff challenges from competitors, like banks and insurance companies, experts said.

Fidelity Investments is in first place, with about $120 billion in 401k assets under management, Vanguard Group Inc, is second, with $80 billion; and State Street Boston Corp third, with about $57 billion, according to the firms. The other leaders are Prudential Insurance Co of America, about $36 billion, and Metropolitan Life Insurance Co, about $35 billion.

Pension experts expect the growth to be into stock funds. "I think you'll see greater diversification into equity-based funds," said Paul Yakoboski, a research associate at the Washington-based Employee Benefit Research Institute.
"The general consensus among providers is when you look at the big picture, many workers tend to be too conservative with their investments."

A sizeable portion of workers's assets are still flowing to fixed-income and money market investments rather than stock funds, even though many plan providers feel stocks offer better returns over the long term.
"Workers are sacrificing retirement income down the road," Yakoboski said.
But the trend has been shifting. About 73.1 percent of contributions went into equity funds in 1996, up from 64.4 percent in 1994, according to Access Research.
The next biggest piece of the pie was stable value funds, but that fell to 14.5 percent in 1996 from 17.8 percent in 1994.
The remaining assets were invested in such vehicles as company stock, guaranteed income contracts (GICs), and commingled trust funds, according to Cerulli.

In another indication of expected growth in 401k plans -- funds based on defined contributions were seen surpassing funds based on defined benefits, predominantly provided by the company, within the next few years, according to pension experts.
In 1996, assets from defined benefit schemes were forecast at about $1.86 trillion versus about $1.37 trillion in defined contribution assets, according to Access Research.
Banks and insurers, which traditionally offered much of the institutional pension product, are already fighting back, in part by marketing their own or third-party mutual funds.

Some pension fund analysts said institutional money management competitors may soon gain an advantage. "As assets grow larger, institutional funds make sense over mutual funds because of the lower expenses," said Stacy Schaus, a defined contribution consultant at Hewitt Associates in Chicago.

Schaus said institutional funds keep their costs down by not having the same regulatory and distribution expenses as retail funds. The average large-cap retail mutual fund has an expense ratio of 88 basis points for each dollar of assets, compared to 64 basis points for an institutional commingled fund, according to Schaus.

Meanwhile, corporate 401k sponsors have been able to wrangle such investor-friendly features as greater choice of funds, flexibility in switching between funds, and a higher level of customer service.
According to Access Research, the average number of investment choices has risen to 6.3 in 1996 from 4.6 in 1994.
Experts expect that corporate pension providers are beginning to focus on other issues, such as squeezing out the lowest expenses and offer individual financial advice.
The battle will come as company sponsors worry about how the assets are being handled.
"With some of the larger plans, we're definitely hearing real concerns for spending participants money," said Schaus.
"In their fiduciary role, they want to be sure the offering plan is as competitive as possible...They're very conscious of how much participants are paying for the overall plan."
Pressures to lower expenses will intensify. "You're going to see radical pricing shifts in products," said Peter Davis, a partner at management consultng firm Booz Allen.
